Question 1 Chemistry of Element X (28 points, 12%)
X was first discovered in 1898 and is widely used in the electronics and electric-light-source industries. It is relatively unreactive and exhibits several oxidation states in its compounds. Common fluorides of X include A, B, and C, all colorless crystals at room temperature, with the mass fraction of fluorine increasing in that order.

subquestions.text_open:
1.1 A, B, and C can all be prepared by reacting elemental X with fluorine under suitable conditions. A is soluble in water and reacts slowly with it. At 275 ℃, A reacts with CrO_2F_2 to form D, which contains 41.6% Cr. B hydrolyzes rapidly in water and undergoes disproportionation to produce two gases; at 273.15 K and 100 kPa, the gas mixture has a density of 3.91 g·L^-1. Complete hydrolysis of C gives an explosive oxide of X.
1.1.2 Write the equations for the reaction of A with $CrO_2F_2$ to form D and for the reaction of B with water.

1.1.3 Dry A and B can both be stored in glass containers, but placing C in a glass or quartz container, whose principal component may be taken as $SiO_2$, is highly dangerous. Use a chemical equation to explain why C cannot be stored in a quartz container.

1.2 In addition to forming covalent compounds with elements such as fluorine and oxygen, X forms a rich variety of ionic compounds. The earliest reported X-containing anion can be prepared as follows: C hydrolyzes and disproportionates under basic conditions to give two gases and octahedral anion E. In addition, C reacts with an equimolar amount of CsF to give F; heating F converts it to G, in which the mass fraction of X is 23.91%.
1.2.2 In the X-containing anions above, the X–O and X–F distances are close to the sums of the corresponding covalent radii, indicating covalent bonding. In some X-containing anions discovered later, however, the X–halogen distance is substantially longer than the sum of the covalent radii but shorter than the sum of the van der Waals radii. To explain this observation, scientists proposed the concept of an X bond (AeB). When X is bonded to a highly electronegative element or electron-withdrawing group, its electron distribution changes markedly, creating a region of high electrostatic potential along the extension of the $\sigma$-bond axis, a $\sigma$ hole. X thereby acts as an electrophilic center that can interact with nucleophiles such as halide ions.
1.2.2.1 F hydrolyzes slowly in moist air to give H, whose formula may be regarded as an adduct of an oxide of X with $CsF$. In the crystal, the anion of H forms an infinite one-dimensional chain. Write its SMILES string.
1.2.2.2 In the presence of $CsF$, partial hydrolysis of C gives I. I contains 47.93% X by mass, and all X atoms have the same chemical environment. Write the SMILES string for the anion of I.

1.3 The physical properties of A, B, and C have also been studied extensively. Researchers measured the standard equilibrium constants of the following reactions at several temperatures; all species are gaseous and treated as ideal gases.

| Temperature (℃) / Reaction | 250 | 300 | 350 | 400 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X + F_2 \rightarrow A$ | $8.79\times10^{4}$ | $1.02\times10^{4}$ | $1.67\times10^{3}$ | $3.59\times10^{2}$ |
| $A + F_2 \rightarrow B$ | $1.43\times10^{3}$ | $1.55\times10^{2}$ | 27.2 | 4.86 |
| $B + F_2 \rightarrow C$ | 0.944 | 0.211 | 0.0558 | 0.0182 |

1.3.1 Calculate $\Delta_r H_m^θ$ and $\Delta_r S_m^θ$ for each reaction, assuming $\Delta_r H_m^θ$ and $\Delta_r S_m^θ$ are temperature-independent.
1.3.3 At 300 ℃, 1 mol of X and 5 mol of $F_2$ are introduced into a 1 L vessel. Calculate the mole fraction of C in the equilibrium gas mixture.
